content.title: About
content.content: Chicken tenders or strips are pieces of chicken breast meat coated in a seasoned breadcrumb mixture and fried or baked until golden and crispy. They are a common menu item in fast‑food restaurants, served as a snack or part of a main dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The coating usually contains a blend of wheat flour, spices, and sometimes dried white‑bread crumbs.
Chicken tenders became popular in the United States in the 1970s and quickly spread worldwide.
For extra crunch, some restaurants use a double coating – a light flour dip, then an egg wash, and a second breadcrumb layer.
Gluten‑free versions are available, using corn starch or rice flour instead of wheat.
They are often served with dipping sauces such as barbecue, honey‑mustard, cheese, or spicy sriracha.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Chicken provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low fat when baked
items.content: Baking or air‑frying reduces saturated fat compared with deep‑frying.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken is a good source of niacin (B3) and pyridoxine (B6), supporting metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Contains phosphorus, selenium and zinc, important for bone health and immunity.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: The tender texture makes them suitable for children and people with chewing difficulties.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Seasoned breading often adds salt, which can raise blood pressure if consumed in excess.

items.title: Trans fats and saturated fats
items.content: Deep‑frying can create trans fats that are harmful to cardiovascular health.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional breading contains wheat; gluten‑intolerant individuals should choose gluten‑free options.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Because of the coating and cooking method, tenders can be calorie‑rich; portion control is advised.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Undercooked chicken may harbor salmonella; ensure internal temperature reaches 75 °C (165 °F).

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve hot with dipping sauces. They can be added to salads, wraps, or enjoyed as a protein‑rich snack between meals.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked tenders in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Frozen tenders last up to 2 months; reheat thoroughly before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Egg salad with creamy dressing is a classic mid‑20th‑century dish. It is made from hard‑boiled eggs mixed with mayonnaise or sour cream, often with mustard, herbs, and spices. Served cold as a snack or side.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first recipes for creamy egg salad appeared in American cookbooks in the 1950s.
The salad was a popular quick lunch for soldiers and schoolchildren.
In Soviet versions, pickles or sauerkraut were sometimes added.
Creamy dressing can be based on mayo, sour cream, or yogurt, altering the flavor profile.
Egg salad is a staple at picnics and barbecues because it transports easily.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Eggs provide complete protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs contain B12, riboflavin, and folate, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Source of healthy fats
items.content: When the dressing uses olive‑oil‑based mayo, it adds monounsaturated fats beneficial for heart health.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Eggs supply iron, zinc, and selenium, important for immunity and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Promotes satiety
items.content: The combination of protein and fat helps keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to eggs, ranging from mild to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Risk of salmonella
items.content: Undercooked eggs can harbor salmonella; ensure eggs are fully hard‑boiled.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Creamy dressing adds significant calories and fat, so portion size should be monitored.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Egg yolks contain cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should consume in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the egg salad cold as a snack, on sandwiches, toast, or as a side to meat dishes. Garnish with fresh herbs, paprika, or avocado slices for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3–4 days. For longer storage, add the dressing just before serving to prevent the eggs from becoming soggy.

content.title: About
content.content: Tzatziki dip is a traditional Greek sauce made from yogurt, cucumbers, garlic, olive oil, dill, and spices. It has a refreshing, slightly tangy flavor and a creamy texture, perfect with vegetables, bread, meat, and fish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name tzatziki comes from the Greek word “τζατζίκι,” meaning “yogurt sauce.”
The original recipe uses thick Greek yogurt, which is richer and less acidic than regular yogurt.
Tzatziki is commonly served with grilled dishes such as souvlaki and gyros.
Some regional variations add mint or lemon juice for extra freshness.
It is considered a low‑calorie sauce suitable for diet-friendly meals.

items.title: Rich in probiotics
items.content: Greek yogurt contains live cultures that support gut health.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Tzatziki typically provides about 50–70 kcal per 100 g, making it a good choice for weight control.

items.title: Source of calcium and protein
items.content: The yogurt supplies calcium for bones and protein for muscles.

items.title: Antioxidants from cucumber and dill
items.content: Cucumber and dill contain vitamins C and K as well as antioxidants that help protect cells.

items.title: Hydration support
items.content: Cucumbers are over 95 % water, aiding overall hydration.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Yogurt contains lactose, so those with intolerance should choose lactose‑free versions.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: Tzatziki can trigger reactions in individuals allergic to dairy.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some recipes add salt; people monitoring sodium intake should adjust accordingly.

items.title: Shelf life
items.content: Because it contains fresh ingredients, the dip spoils quickly; keep it refrigerated and consume within a few days.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve tzatziki as a dip with fresh veggies, pita bread, or lavash, and as a sauce for grilled meats, fish, potatoes, and rice dishes. It also works well as a salad dressing.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store tzatziki in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C. It keeps for 3–5 days. Discard if it develops a sour smell or changes color.
